High Conflict Dynamics
Parenting
A pattern of persistent, entrenched hostility between separated parents that affects co-parenting capacity and exposes children to ongoing conflict.
When it applies: This applies when parenting arrangements are being negotiated, documented, or decided by the court. The focus remains on the child's best interests, safety, stability, and the practical realities of each family.
High Conflict Parenting
Parenting
An entrenched pattern of conflict between separated parents that significantly impairs their ability to co-parent effectively and, in serious cases, causes harm to the children involved. High-conflict matters often involve repeated litigation, allegations, and inability to implement court orders.
When it applies: This applies when parenting arrangements are being negotiated, documented, or decided by the court. The focus remains on the child's best interests, safety, stability, and the practical realities of each family.
High-Conflict Personality Allegation
High Conflict
A claim that one party exhibits entrenched, controlling, or manipulative behaviour patterns consistent with a high-conflict personality, often raised in the context of family violence or coercive control allegations.
When it applies: This applies where conflict is persistent, communication is unsafe or unproductive, or one party's behaviour affects compliance, parenting, or settlement. Courts look for practical arrangements that reduce risk and protect children from adult conflict.

In Camera Proceedings
Court Administration
Proceedings held in private, closed to the public and the media. Family law proceedings are presumptively in camera under section 97 of the Family Law Act to protect the privacy of children and parties.
When it applies: This applies when dealing with the registry, court records, filing systems, listings, sealed documents, or practical case management. It is usually procedural, but mistakes can still delay a matter.
Incident Weighting
Evidence
The court's assessment of the seriousness and relevance of specific events described in the evidence. Not all incidents carry equal weight — courts assess frequency, severity, impact, and context.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.
Inconsistent Evidence
Evidence
Evidence that conflicts with the same party's prior statements, documents, or conduct. Inconsistencies — whether between affidavits, between oral evidence and affidavit material, or between evidence and documents — undermine a party's credibility.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.
Indemnity Costs
Court Process
The highest category of costs orders, requiring a party to pay the other party's legal costs on a dollar-for-dollar basis — as opposed to the standard party-party costs, which cover only a portion of actual costs. Indemnity costs are ordered where a party's conduct has been particularly unreasonable or blameworthy.
When it applies: This applies when the term appears in family law documents, court directions, legal correspondence, or conversations about resolving a case.
Independent Children's Lawyer
Court Administration
A lawyer appointed by the court to represent the best interests of a child in family law proceedings, independent of both parents. The ICL does not take instructions from the child but advocates for the child's best interests as an independent voice.
When it applies: This applies when dealing with the registry, court records, filing systems, listings, sealed documents, or practical case management. It is usually procedural, but mistakes can still delay a matter.
Independent Children's Lawyer (ICL)
Parenting
A lawyer appointed by the court to independently represent the best interests of a child in contested parenting proceedings. The ICL does not act on the child's instructions but advocates for what they independently assess to be in the child's best interests, based on all available information.
When it applies: This applies when parenting arrangements are being negotiated, documented, or decided by the court. The focus remains on the child's best interests, safety, stability, and the practical realities of each family.
Independent Children's Lawyer (ICL) Appointment Power
Legislation
The legislative authority allowing the court to appoint an Independent Children's Lawyer to represent a child's interests in proceedings. Under section 68L of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), the court may make this appointment on its own initiative or on application, where it is in the interests of the child to do so.
When it applies: This applies when the answer depends on a statute, rule, regulation, or formal legal test. It helps distinguish practical guidance from the legal source of a power or requirement.

Orders

Court Process
Temporary rules or orders governing how separated parents must communicate during proceedings, designed to reduce conflict and protect the parties and children from harmful interactions.

Orders

Orders

When it applies: This applies when asking the court to make, change, enforce, suspend, or clarify an order. The wording of proposed orders matters because it affects whether obligations are clear and enforceable.
Interim Risk Assessment
Court Process
An evaluation of the immediate risks to a child or party conducted at the interim stage, before full evidence is available. It informs the orders the court makes to protect safety while proceedings continue.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Interim Risk Assessment helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Interim Stability Consideration
Court Process
The court's focus, when making interim parenting orders, on minimising disruption and uncertainty for children while proceedings are ongoing. Stability of routine, relationships, and schooling is given significant weight.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Interim Stability Consideration helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Interim Without Findings
Court Process
Interim orders made by a court without determining the truth of the allegations before it. The court acts to protect safety or preserve the status quo without making factual findings, which are reserved for the final hearing.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Interim Without Findings helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.

Court Administration

Investment Property Disclosure is a financial concept relevant to property settlement, disclosure, maintenance, child support, debts, assets, superannuation, income, or valuation. It helps explain how financial issues are identified and dealt with after separation.
When it applies: This applies when parties are identifying the asset pool, exchanging disclosure, valuing property, assessing contributions, considering future needs, or resolving financial support issues. Accurate documents and complete disclosure are important.

Joint Application for Divorce
Court Process
Joint Application for Divorce is a procedural concept or step used in Australian family law proceedings. It helps identify what must be filed, served, listed, answered, or decided as the matter moves through court.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Joint Application for Divorce helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.

Judge
Court Administration
A judicial officer of the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (FCFCOA) who presides over family law proceedings, hears evidence, and makes binding orders. Judges are addressed as 'Your Honour' in court.
When it applies: This applies when dealing with the registry, court records, filing systems, listings, sealed documents, or practical case management. It is usually procedural, but mistakes can still delay a matter.
Judgment
Court Process
The formal written or oral decision of the court delivered by a judge at the conclusion of a hearing or trial. It sets out findings of fact, the reasoning applied, the legal conclusions reached, and the orders made.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Judgment helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Judicial Registrar
Court Administration
A judicial officer of the Federal Circuit and Family Court who exercises delegated powers from a judge. Judicial Registrars conduct procedural hearings, consent orders, and some defended hearings.
When it applies: This applies when dealing with the registry, court records, filing systems, listings, sealed documents, or practical case management. It is usually procedural, but mistakes can still delay a matter.
Judicial Settlement Conference
Court Process
A settlement conference presided over by a judge or senior judicial officer, at which the parties attempt to resolve their dispute with the assistance of the court. The judge plays an active facilitative role but does not impose a decision.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Judicial Settlement Conference helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Jurisdiction
Legislation
The legal authority of a particular court to hear and decide a matter. In Australian family law, jurisdiction is conferred by the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) and related legislation. Without jurisdiction, a court has no power to make orders.
When it applies: This applies when the answer depends on a statute, rule, regulation, or formal legal test. It helps distinguish practical guidance from the legal source of a power or requirement.
Just and Equitable
Orders
The overarching requirement that any property settlement order must be just and equitable in all the circumstances. Even if contributions and future needs calculations suggest a particular outcome, the court has a discretion to adjust if the result would be unjust.
When it applies: This applies when asking the court to make, change, enforce, suspend, or clarify an order. The wording of proposed orders matters because it affects whether obligations are clear and enforceable.

Late Return Allegation
High Conflict
A claim that a parent returned a child to the other parent later than required by the parenting order, without reasonable excuse or prior agreement.
When it applies: This applies where conflict is persistent, communication is unsafe or unproductive, or one party's behaviour affects compliance, parenting, or settlement. Courts look for practical arrangements that reduce risk and protect children from adult conflict.
Lawyer-Assisted Mediation
Dispute Resolution
Lawyer-Assisted Mediation is part of resolving family law issues without, or before, a contested final hearing. It may involve mediation, negotiation, family dispute resolution, conciliation, settlement offers, or narrowing issues in dispute.
When it applies: This applies when parties are trying to resolve issues by agreement or narrow the dispute before a hearing. It is often cheaper, faster, and less stressful than litigating every issue.
Leave of Court
Court Administration
Permission granted by a court to take a step in proceedings that would otherwise not be permitted — for example, to file a document out of time, adduce additional evidence, or amend an application.
When it applies: This applies when dealing with the registry, court records, filing systems, listings, sealed documents, or practical case management. It is usually procedural, but mistakes can still delay a matter.
Leave of the Court
Court Process
Permission granted by the court to take a procedural step that would not otherwise be allowed as of right. Leave may be required to file documents out of time, to appeal, to call additional witnesses, or to take any other step for which the rules require judicial approval.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Leave of the Court helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Leave to Appeal
Court Process
Permission from a court to bring an appeal. In the family law jurisdiction, leave is required before most appeals to the Full Court of the FCFCOA can be filed. Leave is granted where the appeal has reasonable prospects of success or raises an issue of general principle.
When it applies: This applies when the term appears in family law documents, court directions, legal correspondence, or conversations about resolving a case.
Leave to File Out of Time
Court Administration
Permission granted by the court to accept documents that have been, or will be, lodged after the prescribed deadline. It is a specific form of leave addressing the court's procedural rules about filing timeframes.
When it applies: This applies when dealing with the registry, court records, filing systems, listings, sealed documents, or practical case management. It is usually procedural, but mistakes can still delay a matter.

Legislative Amendment
Legislation
A formal change made to an Act of Parliament that alters how the law operates. Amendments may add, remove, or modify provisions. The Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) has been amended many times, most significantly in 2006 and again in 2023, each time substantially changing how parenting matters are decided.
When it applies: This applies when the answer depends on a statute, rule, regulation, or formal legal test. It helps distinguish practical guidance from the legal source of a power or requirement.
Liberty to Apply
Orders
A provision within court orders allowing either party to return to the court on short notice to address a specific practical difficulty or dispute about the implementation of the orders, without needing to file a fresh application.
When it applies: This applies when asking the court to make, change, enforce, suspend, or clarify an order. The wording of proposed orders matters because it affects whether obligations are clear and enforceable.

Limited Evidence Hearing
Court Process
A hearing conducted primarily on the basis of written affidavit material, with limited or no oral evidence and cross-examination. Most interim hearings in family law are limited evidence hearings.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Limited Evidence Hearing helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Listing
Court Administration
The scheduling of a matter for a particular hearing type on a specific date. A matter may be listed for a mention, a directions hearing, an interim hearing, a conciliation conference, or a final hearing. Listings are managed by the court registry.
When it applies: This applies when dealing with the registry, court records, filing systems, listings, sealed documents, or practical case management. It is usually procedural, but mistakes can still delay a matter.

Litigation Abuse
Court Process
The use of legal proceedings as a tool of harassment, intimidation or financial attrition. Recognised as a form of post-separation family violence.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Litigation Abuse helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Litigation Abuse Condition
Protection
Litigation Abuse Condition relates to safety, family violence, risk, or protective conditions in family law and related AVO proceedings. It can affect parenting arrangements, evidence, urgency, and the court's approach to risk management.
When it applies: This applies where there are allegations or concerns about violence, intimidation, coercive control, harassment, child safety, or immediate risk. Protective concerns should be raised clearly and supported with specific evidence where available.

Litigation Fatigue
High Conflict
The emotional and financial exhaustion experienced by parties involved in prolonged, high-conflict family law proceedings. It can lead to poor decision-making, settlement under duress, and significant harm to the parties and their children.
When it applies: This applies where conflict is persistent, communication is unsafe or unproductive, or one party's behaviour affects compliance, parenting, or settlement. Courts look for practical arrangements that reduce risk and protect children from adult conflict.
Litigation Guardian
Court Process
A person appointed by the court to conduct proceedings on behalf of a party who lacks legal capacity — such as a person with a significant cognitive disability or mental illness. The litigation guardian acts in the party's best interests rather than on their instructions.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Litigation Guardian helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Litigation Positioning
High Conflict
The strategic framing of facts, allegations, and legal arguments to strengthen a party's position in proceedings, rather than to present events neutrally.
When it applies: This applies where conflict is persistent, communication is unsafe or unproductive, or one party's behaviour affects compliance, parenting, or settlement. Courts look for practical arrangements that reduce risk and protect children from adult conflict.
Live With (Order)
Parenting
A parenting order specifying the parent or parents with whom a child will primarily live. It replaced the older terminology of "residence order" and is used in conjunction with "spend time with" orders to describe the overall parenting arrangement.

Lump Sum Costs
Court Process
A costs order that specifies a fixed total amount the paying party must pay, rather than requiring a detailed assessment of every item of legal work. Lump sum orders provide certainty and avoid the cost and delay of a formal costs assessment.
When it applies: This applies when the term appears in family law documents, court directions, legal correspondence, or conversations about resolving a case.

Magistrate

Major Long-Term Issues
Parenting
Significant decisions about a child's upbringing that have lasting impact and are not routine day-to-day decisions. Under the Family Law Act, major long-term issues include education, religious upbringing, health care, name, and changes to living arrangements that make it significantly more difficult for the child to spend time with a parent.
When it applies: This applies when parenting arrangements are being negotiated, documented, or decided by the court. The focus remains on the child's best interests, safety, stability, and the practical realities of each family.

Parenting

Mandatory Conditions
Protection
The standard conditions that are automatically included in every AVO in NSW, regardless of the specific circumstances. These cannot be removed by the court — they apply to all AVOs without exception.
When it applies: This applies where there are allegations or concerns about violence, intimidation, coercive control, harassment, child safety, or immediate risk. Protective concerns should be raised clearly and supported with specific evidence where available.
Mandatory Report Condition
Protection
Mandatory Report Condition relates to safety, family violence, risk, or protective conditions in family law and related AVO proceedings. It can affect parenting arrangements, evidence, urgency, and the court's approach to risk management.

Mandatory Reporting
Protection
The legal obligation on specified categories of professionals to report to child protection authorities when they reasonably suspect a child is being abused or is at risk of harm. Mandatory reporting obligations exist under state and territory legislation throughout Australia.
When it applies: This applies where there are allegations or concerns about violence, intimidation, coercive control, harassment, child safety, or immediate risk. Protective concerns should be raised clearly and supported with specific evidence where available.
Mandatory Reporting Obligations
Legislation
Legal requirements imposed on certain professionals — including teachers, doctors, nurses, and social workers — to report suspected child abuse or neglect to the relevant authority. Mandatory reporting laws are set by state and territory legislation, not the Family Law Act, but reports made under these laws can intersect significantly with family law proceedings.
When it applies: This applies when the answer depends on a statute, rule, regulation, or formal legal test. It helps distinguish practical guidance from the legal source of a power or requirement.
Mareva Injunction
Orders
An urgent court order freezing a party's assets to prevent them from being dissipated, hidden, or transferred before a final court order can be made. Named after Mareva Compania Naviera SA v International Bulkcarriers SA [1975].
When it applies: This applies when asking the court to make, change, enforce, suspend, or clarify an order. The wording of proposed orders matters because it affects whether obligations are clear and enforceable.

Material Change in Circumstances
Court Process
A significant change in circumstances since final parenting orders were made that justifies the court reconsidering those orders. The change must be substantial — not merely a routine life development or minor dissatisfaction — and must have occurred after the orders were finalised.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Material Change in Circumstances helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Material Facts
Evidence
Facts that are directly relevant to the issues in dispute and which could affect the outcome of the proceedings. All parties have an obligation to disclose material facts, including those that may be unhelpful to their own case.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.
Matter Number
Court Administration
See Case Number. The unique identifier assigned to a family law matter upon filing, used to track and identify the proceedings throughout their life.
When it applies: This applies when dealing with the registry, court records, filing systems, listings, sealed documents, or practical case management. It is usually procedural, but mistakes can still delay a matter.
McKenzie Friend
Court Administration
A person who assists a self-represented litigant in court proceedings by taking notes, helping organise documents, and providing moral support. A McKenzie friend does not appear as an advocate and does not address the court.
When it applies: This applies when dealing with the registry, court records, filing systems, listings, sealed documents, or practical case management. It is usually procedural, but mistakes can still delay a matter.

Mediation
Dispute Resolution
A structured, confidential process in which a neutral third party (the mediator) facilitates communication between disputing parties to help them reach a voluntary agreement. The mediator does not impose a decision. Any agreement only becomes binding if formalised as consent orders or a financial agreement.
When it applies: This applies when parties are trying to resolve issues by agreement or narrow the dispute before a hearing. It is often cheaper, faster, and less stressful than litigating every issue.
Mediation Intake
Dispute Resolution
The preliminary assessment stage conducted by a Family Dispute Resolution practitioner before mediation commences. During intake, the practitioner meets separately with each party to assess whether the matter is suitable for FDR, identify safety concerns, and explain the process.
When it applies: This applies when parties are trying to resolve issues by agreement or narrow the dispute before a hearing. It is often cheaper, faster, and less stressful than litigating every issue.

Mention
Court Process
A brief procedural court appearance, usually before a registrar, at which the progress of the matter is reviewed, directions are given, and the next steps are confirmed. It is administrative in nature and does not involve the hearing of substantive evidence.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Mention helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Mention Date
Court Process
A court date on which a matter is briefly reviewed to confirm its status, give procedural directions, or check that parties have complied with earlier orders. A mention is shorter than a hearing and usually does not involve evidence.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Mention Date helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Mentions Hearing
Court Process
A brief procedural court appearance at which the court reviews the status of a matter, confirms what has been filed, and gives directions about the next steps. A mentions hearing does not involve the giving of evidence.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Mentions Hearing helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.

Message Misinterpretation
High Conflict
A dispute arising from different understandings of the meaning, tone, or intent of a written communication between parties. In high-conflict matters, message misinterpretation is a frequent source of satellite litigation.
When it applies: This applies where conflict is persistent, communication is unsafe or unproductive, or one party's behaviour affects compliance, parenting, or settlement. Courts look for practical arrangements that reduce risk and protect children from adult conflict.

Minute of Proposed Orders
Court Process
A document setting out the precise wording of the orders a party is asking the court to make, drafted in the form that the orders would take if granted, and presented to the court before or at the hearing.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Minute of Proposed Orders helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Mirror Order
Parenting
An order made by a court in a foreign country that mirrors the terms of an Australian parenting order, enforceable in that jurisdiction. Mirror orders are used where children travel or live internationally, ensuring the Australian orders are recognised and enforceable abroad.
When it applies: This applies when parenting arrangements are being negotiated, documented, or decided by the court. The focus remains on the child's best interests, safety, stability, and the practical realities of each family.

Parallel Parenting
Parenting
A structured post-separation parenting model designed for high-conflict situations, in which each parent operates independently in their own domain with minimal direct communication. It reduces conflict by limiting the need for cooperative co-parenting.

Paramountcy Principle
Legislation
The foundational legal principle that the child's best interests are the most important — or paramount — consideration in all parenting decisions made by the court. Enshrined in section 60CA of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), the paramountcy principle overrides other considerations, including the preferences of either parent.

When it applies: This applies when parenting arrangements are being negotiated, documented, or decided by the court. The focus remains on the child's best interests, safety, stability, and the practical realities of each family.

Dispute Resolution
An agreement by which a trained parenting coordinator is engaged to assist high-conflict parents implement their parenting orders, manage day-to-day disputes, and improve communication. Within their agreed scope, a parenting coordinator may make recommendations or minor decisions.

When it applies: This applies when parenting arrangements are being negotiated, documented, or decided by the court. The focus remains on the child's best interests, safety, stability, and the practical realities of each family.

Parenting

When it applies: This applies when parenting arrangements are being negotiated, documented, or decided by the court. The focus remains on the child's best interests, safety, stability, and the practical realities of each family.

Parenting

When it applies: This applies when parenting arrangements are being negotiated, documented, or decided by the court. The focus remains on the child's best interests, safety, stability, and the practical realities of each family.
Parenting Plan
Parenting
A written agreement between parents about their child's living arrangements and related matters, made without court involvement. Parenting plans are flexible and can be amended by written agreement, but they are not legally enforceable as they have not been approved by a court.
When it applies: This applies when parenting arrangements are being negotiated, documented, or decided by the court. The focus remains on the child's best interests, safety, stability, and the practical realities of each family.
Particulars
Evidence
Specific factual details provided in support of a claim or allegation — including dates, places, descriptions of incidents, and their alleged effects. Particulars give substance and precision to allegations that might otherwise be too vague to respond to or assess.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.
Party-Party Costs
Court Process
The standard basis for costs orders in family law proceedings, under which the paying party contributes to — but does not fully cover — the other party's legal costs. Party-party costs are typically 60-70% of actual legal costs.
When it applies: This applies when the term appears in family law documents, court directions, legal correspondence, or conversations about resolving a case.

Pattern Evidence
Evidence
Evidence demonstrating a consistent course of behaviour over time rather than relying on a single incident. Particularly significant in family violence and coercive control contexts.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.
Pattern of Intimidation
Protection
Repeated behaviour — such as threats, aggressive communication, physical presence, property damage, or surveillance — that causes a person to fear for their safety. A pattern is more probative than isolated incidents.
When it applies: This applies where there are allegations or concerns about violence, intimidation, coercive control, harassment, child safety, or immediate risk. Protective concerns should be raised clearly and supported with specific evidence where available.
Pattern of Non-Compliance
Orders
A series of failures to comply with court orders over time, demonstrating an entrenched disregard for the court's authority. Courts treat a pattern more seriously than an isolated breach.
When it applies: This applies when asking the court to make, change, enforce, suspend, or clarify an order. The wording of proposed orders matters because it affects whether obligations are clear and enforceable.

Parenting
The arrangements, communication, and practical cooperation by which separated parents continue to raise their children. It encompasses both the legal framework (parenting orders and plans) and the day-to-day reality of managing a child's life across two households.
When it applies: This applies when parenting arrangements are being negotiated, documented, or decided by the court. The focus remains on the child's best interests, safety, stability, and the practical realities of each family.

Court Administration

When it applies: This applies when dealing with the registry, court records, filing systems, listings, sealed documents, or practical case management. It is usually procedural, but mistakes can still delay a matter.
Presumption of Equal Shared Parental Responsibility
Legislation
A starting legal assumption — formerly in the Family Law Act — that both parents should share equal responsibility for major long-term decisions about a child's life. This presumption was repealed by the 2023 amendments to the Family Law Act and no longer applies. Courts now consider parental responsibility as part of the broader best interests assessment without any presumption.
When it applies: This applies when the answer depends on a statute, rule, regulation, or formal legal test. It helps distinguish practical guidance from the legal source of a power or requirement.

Evidence

Primary Considerations
Legislation
The most important factors a court must consider under legislation when determining a child's best interests. Under the amended Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), the primary considerations are: (1) the benefit to the child of having a meaningful relationship with both parents; and (2) the need to protect the child from harm, including family violence, abuse, and neglect. Where these considerations conflict, safety takes priority.
When it applies: This applies when the answer depends on a statute, rule, regulation, or formal legal test. It helps distinguish practical guidance from the legal source of a power or requirement.

Probative Value
Evidence
The capacity of a piece of evidence to prove or disprove a fact in issue. High probative value means the evidence significantly advances the case on a material point. Courts weigh probative value against other considerations such as prejudice and reliability.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.
Procedural Fairness
Legislation
The legislative and common law requirement that parties be given a fair opportunity to present their case and respond to allegations before a decision is made. Also called natural justice. A decision made without procedural fairness can be set aside on appeal.
When it applies: This applies when the answer depends on a statute, rule, regulation, or formal legal test. It helps distinguish practical guidance from the legal source of a power or requirement.
Procedural Fairness (Natural Justice)
Court Process
The fundamental legal requirement that each party in proceedings is given a fair opportunity to be heard and to have their evidence and arguments genuinely considered before a decision is made. It also requires the court to act without bias.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Procedural Fairness (Natural Justice) helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Procedural Fairness at Interim Stage
Court Process
The obligation on the court to ensure both parties have a meaningful opportunity to be heard before interim orders are made, even when time is limited. It includes adequate notice and the chance to file responding material.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Procedural Fairness at Interim Stage helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Procedural Obstruction
High Conflict
Deliberate non-cooperation or obstruction of the court's procedural steps — such as refusing to file documents on time, failing to attend conferences, or withholding disclosure — in a way that impedes the progress of proceedings.
When it applies: This applies where conflict is persistent, communication is unsafe or unproductive, or one party's behaviour affects compliance, parenting, or settlement. Courts look for practical arrangements that reduce risk and protect children from adult conflict.
Procedural Order
Court Process
A court order managing the steps and timetable for a case — including filing deadlines, exchange of documents, attendance at conferences, or commissioning expert reports. Procedural orders organise proceedings rather than determining their outcome.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Procedural Order helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Procedural Threshold
Court Process
A minimum legal requirement that must be satisfied before a court will proceed with an application or consider varying existing orders.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Procedural Threshold helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.

Profit And Loss Statement Valuation is a financial concept relevant to property settlement, disclosure, maintenance, child support, debts, assets, superannuation, income, or valuation. It helps explain how financial issues are identified and dealt with after separation.
When it applies: This applies when parties are identifying the asset pool, exchanging disclosure, valuing property, assessing contributions, considering future needs, or resolving financial support issues. Accurate documents and complete disclosure are important.

Orders

When it applies: This applies when asking the court to make, change, enforce, suspend, or clarify an order. The wording of proposed orders matters because it affects whether obligations are clear and enforceable.
Proof of Service
Court Process
Documentary evidence that a party has been formally served with court documents — such as an application, orders, or a subpoena. Proof of service is usually an affidavit of service sworn by the person who effected service.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Proof of Service helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.

Property Settlement

When it applies: This applies when asking the court to make, change, enforce, suspend, or clarify an order. The wording of proposed orders matters because it affects whether obligations are clear and enforceable.
Proportional Response
Court Process
The principle that legal steps taken in proceedings should be appropriate in scale and cost to the nature and significance of the issue in dispute. Disproportionate litigation responses are contrary to the overarching purpose of the FCFCOA Act.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Proportional Response helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Protected Address
Protection
The residential, work, or other address of the protected person that is named in the AVO as a location the defendant must not approach or enter.

Protected Person
Protection
The individual — or individuals — named in an AVO as the person or persons whose safety the order is designed to protect. The AVO imposes restrictions on the defendant's conduct specifically in relation to the protected person.

Parenting

Pseudonym Order
Court Process

Psychological Abuse
High Conflict
A form of family violence involving the use of threats, humiliation, intimidation, and emotional manipulation to control or harm another person. Psychological abuse does not require physical contact and is recognised as family violence under Australian law.
When it applies: This applies where conflict is persistent, communication is unsafe or unproductive, or one party's behaviour affects compliance, parenting, or settlement. Courts look for practical arrangements that reduce risk and protect children from adult conflict.
Psychological Safety Consideration
Protection
The court's evaluation of a child's or party's emotional wellbeing and psychological security in the context of proposed parenting or protective arrangements. It extends beyond physical safety to include mental health and emotional stability.
When it applies: This applies where there are allegations or concerns about violence, intimidation, coercive control, harassment, child safety, or immediate risk. Protective concerns should be raised clearly and supported with specific evidence where available.

Re-Examination
Evidence
The questioning of a witness by the party who called them, conducted after that witness has been cross-examined by the other side. Re-examination is confined to matters arising from cross-examination and cannot introduce new topics.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.
Reactive Allegation
High Conflict
An allegation made in direct response to a claim filed by the other party, rather than arising independently from the facts.
When it applies: This applies where conflict is persistent, communication is unsafe or unproductive, or one party's behaviour affects compliance, parenting, or settlement. Courts look for practical arrangements that reduce risk and protect children from adult conflict.

Court Administration

When it applies: This applies when dealing with the registry, court records, filing systems, listings, sealed documents, or practical case management. It is usually procedural, but mistakes can still delay a matter.
Readiness Hearing
Court Process
Readiness Hearing is a procedural concept or step used in Australian family law proceedings. It helps identify what must be filed, served, listed, answered, or decided as the matter moves through court.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Readiness Hearing helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Reasonable Excuse
Orders
A justification for non-compliance with a court order that the court accepts as sufficient to excuse or mitigate the breach. What constitutes a reasonable excuse depends on the circumstances of each case.
When it applies: This applies when asking the court to make, change, enforce, suspend, or clarify an order. The wording of proposed orders matters because it affects whether obligations are clear and enforceable.
Reasons for Judgment
Court Process
The written explanation provided by a judge setting out the facts found, the law applied, and the reasons for the orders made. Reasons for judgment are a fundamental requirement of procedural fairness — parties are entitled to know why the court decided as it did.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Reasons for Judgment helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Rebuttable Presumption
Legislation
A legal assumption that applies as the starting position in a matter but can be displaced if sufficient evidence is provided to disprove it. In family law, rebuttable presumptions operate as defaults that shift the burden of proof — a party who wishes to displace the presumption must adduce evidence that outweighs it.
When it applies: This applies when the answer depends on a statute, rule, regulation, or formal legal test. It helps distinguish practical guidance from the legal source of a power or requirement.

Recovery Order
Orders
A court order requiring the return of a child to the person with whom they are supposed to be living, following a contravention of a parenting order by the other parent or a third party. Federal Police may be authorised to locate and return the child.
When it applies: This applies when asking the court to make, change, enforce, suspend, or clarify an order. The wording of proposed orders matters because it affects whether obligations are clear and enforceable.
Recovery Order Application
Orders
An application to the court seeking orders for the immediate return of a child who has been wrongfully retained or removed — whether interstate or internationally — in breach of existing parenting orders or without consent.
When it applies: This applies when asking the court to make, change, enforce, suspend, or clarify an order. The wording of proposed orders matters because it affects whether obligations are clear and enforceable.

Relevance
Evidence
A fundamental requirement for evidence to be admissible: the evidence must have a rational connection to a fact that is in issue in the proceedings. Evidence that does not assist in proving or disproving a material fact may be excluded as irrelevant.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.
Relevance Threshold
Evidence
The standard determining whether a piece of evidence has a sufficient connection to the issues in dispute to be admissible or worthy of inclusion. Evidence that does not meet the relevance threshold may be excluded or given no weight.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.

Relocation
Parenting
The proposed move of a parent — and potentially the child — to a location that would significantly affect the child's current parenting arrangements and their relationship with the other parent. Relocation can be interstate or overseas.
When it applies: This applies when parenting arrangements are being negotiated, documented, or decided by the court. The focus remains on the child's best interests, safety, stability, and the practical realities of each family.
Relocation Application
Parenting
A formal application to the court for orders permitting a parent to relocate a child — interstate or overseas — over the other parent's objection. The applicant must demonstrate that relocation is in the child's best interests.
When it applies: This applies when parenting arrangements are being negotiated, documented, or decided by the court. The focus remains on the child's best interests, safety, stability, and the practical realities of each family.
Relocation Objection
Parenting
A formal challenge by one parent to the other parent's proposal to relocate with the child to a different area, whether interstate or internationally. The objecting parent must file an application to restrain the relocation.
When it applies: This applies when parenting arrangements are being negotiated, documented, or decided by the court. The focus remains on the child's best interests, safety, stability, and the practical realities of each family.

Court Process

Restraint Order
Protection
A court order restricting a party from taking specific actions, such as removing a child from a geographic area, disposing of assets, or contacting certain individuals.
When it applies: This applies where there are allegations or concerns about violence, intimidation, coercive control, harassment, child safety, or immediate risk. Protective concerns should be raised clearly and supported with specific evidence where available.
Resulting Trust
Financial
Resulting Trust is a financial concept relevant to property settlement, disclosure, maintenance, child support, debts, assets, superannuation, income, or valuation. It helps explain how financial issues are identified and dealt with after separation.
When it applies: This applies when parties are identifying the asset pool, exchanging disclosure, valuing property, assessing contributions, considering future needs, or resolving financial support issues. Accurate documents and complete disclosure are important.
Retaliatory Allegation
High Conflict
An allegation made in response to a previous complaint or court filing by the other party, appearing designed to neutralise that complaint rather than raising a genuinely independent concern.
When it applies: This applies where conflict is persistent, communication is unsafe or unproductive, or one party's behaviour affects compliance, parenting, or settlement. Courts look for practical arrangements that reduce risk and protect children from adult conflict.
Return of Subpoena
Evidence
The compliance deadline by which a party or third party served with a subpoena must produce the required documents to the court registry.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.
Revocation
Court Process
The formal cancellation of an existing court order — most commonly an AVO, parenting order, or other family law order. An order can only be revoked by another court order, not by private agreement between parties.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Revocation helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Revocation of AVO
Protection
The formal cancellation of an AVO by court order, bringing the order to an end before its expiry date. Revocation requires a court application and is granted at the court's discretion.
When it applies: This applies where there are allegations or concerns about violence, intimidation, coercive control, harassment, child safety, or immediate risk. Protective concerns should be raised clearly and supported with specific evidence where available.
Rice &amp; Asplund Rule
Court Process
A legal principle established in Rice v Asplund (1979) which provides that a court will not reconsider final parenting orders unless there has been a significant change in circumstances since the orders were made. The rule aims to promote stability for children and prevent repeated litigation.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Rice &amp; Asplund Rule helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Risk Assessment
Protection
A structured professional evaluation of the nature and level of risk posed to a child or party. It considers factors such as history of violence, mental health, substance use, and the capacity of each parent to protect the child.
When it applies: This applies where there are allegations or concerns about violence, intimidation, coercive control, harassment, child safety, or immediate risk. Protective concerns should be raised clearly and supported with specific evidence where available.

Risk of Emotional Harm
Protection
An allegation that a child is at risk of psychological or emotional damage as a result of a parent's behaviour, the parenting arrangements, or exposure to conflict. Emotional harm can occur without physical violence.
When it applies: This applies where there are allegations or concerns about violence, intimidation, coercive control, harassment, child safety, or immediate risk. Protective concerns should be raised clearly and supported with specific evidence where available.
Risk of Harm Threshold
Legislation
The minimum level of risk required under legislation before protective intervention — such as supervised contact, a no-contact order, or removal from a parent's care — is legally justified. The threshold is not absolute harm but a real and substantial risk that cannot be adequately managed without court intervention.
When it applies: This applies when the answer depends on a statute, rule, regulation, or formal legal test. It helps distinguish practical guidance from the legal source of a power or requirement.

An allegation that a child or party faces a risk of bodily injury or physical harm. It may relate to past incidents of physical violence or a reasonably apprehended future risk.

Scope of Retainer
Court Administration
Scope of Retainer refers to an administrative part of managing a family law case. It usually concerns registry handling, filing, listing, records, notices, or practical court requirements.
When it applies: This applies when dealing with the registry, court records, filing systems, listings, sealed documents, or practical case management. It is usually procedural, but mistakes can still delay a matter.
Sealed Order
Court Administration
A copy of a court order that has been stamped with the official court seal, making it the enforceable version of the order. Unsealed orders have no enforcement effect.
When it applies: This applies when dealing with the registry, court records, filing systems, listings, sealed documents, or practical case management. It is usually procedural, but mistakes can still delay a matter.
Sealed Orders
Orders
Court orders that have been formally stamped with the court's seal by the registry, confirming they are authorised, final, and issued by the court. The sealed copy is the legally operative document — draft or unsigned versions have no legal effect.
When it applies: This applies when asking the court to make, change, enforce, suspend, or clarify an order. The wording of proposed orders matters because it affects whether obligations are clear and enforceable.
Section 102NA
Protection
A provision of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) that restricts direct cross-examination by an alleged perpetrator of family violence of an alleged victim in family law proceedings.
When it applies: This applies where there are allegations or concerns about violence, intimidation, coercive control, harassment, child safety, or immediate risk. Protective concerns should be raised clearly and supported with specific evidence where available.
Section 117 Costs
Court Process
The provision of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) governing the court's discretion to make costs orders in family law proceedings, including the circumstances in which departure from the usual 'each party bears own costs' rule is justified.
When it applies: This applies when the term appears in family law documents, court directions, legal correspondence, or conversations about resolving a case.
Section 60I Certificate
Court Process
A certificate issued by an accredited Family Dispute Resolution (FDR) practitioner confirming that the parties have attended — or attempted to attend — mediation before commencing parenting proceedings. Required under section 60I of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) before filing most parenting applications.

Stability Argument
Parenting
A submission that maintaining the child's current arrangements — including home, school, community, and relationships — provides important continuity and should be preserved rather than disrupted by proposed changes.
When it applies: This applies when parenting arrangements are being negotiated, documented, or decided by the court. The focus remains on the child's best interests, safety, stability, and the practical realities of each family.
Stalking
Protection
A course of conduct involving repeated following, surveillance, or monitoring of another person that causes that person to fear for their safety. Stalking is a criminal offence in NSW under the Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 and is a common ground for an AVO.
When it applies: This applies where there are allegations or concerns about violence, intimidation, coercive control, harassment, child safety, or immediate risk. Protective concerns should be raised clearly and supported with specific evidence where available.

Stamp
Court Administration
The court's official seal or mark applied to a filed document to confirm that it has been accepted for filing. A stamped copy is the official version of a court document and should be retained by each party. Unstamped copies have no official status.
When it applies: This applies when dealing with the registry, court records, filing systems, listings, sealed documents, or practical case management. It is usually procedural, but mistakes can still delay a matter.
Standard of Proof
Court Process
The level of certainty required by the court.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Standard of Proof helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Statement in Support
Evidence
A written document filed alongside an AVO application setting out the factual basis for seeking the order. It describes the incidents of violence, harassment, or threatening conduct that justify the court granting protection.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.
Statement of Truth
Evidence
A declaration signed by a party confirming that the contents of a document are true and accurate to the best of their knowledge and belief. It is a formal legal obligation, not merely an acknowledgement.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.
Status Quo Principle
Court Process
The general tendency of courts, at the interim stage, to maintain existing arrangements for children rather than making significant changes before full evidence is heard. Stability and continuity are given weight in interim decision-making.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Status Quo Principle helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.

Stay Order
Orders
A court order that temporarily suspends the operation of another court order, typically pending the outcome of an appeal or review. A stay preserves the status quo while the appeal is determined.
When it applies: This applies when asking the court to make, change, enforce, suspend, or clarify an order. The wording of proposed orders matters because it affects whether obligations are clear and enforceable.

Court Process

Parenting
A legislative concept describing a level of parenting time that is less than equal time but still meaningful and substantial. Unacceptable Risk Test
Legislation
A legal test applied by courts to determine whether a child would face an unacceptable risk of harm if particular parenting arrangements were ordered. The test requires the court to weigh the probability and magnitude of the alleged harm against the benefit of the child maintaining a relationship with both parents.
When it applies: This applies when the answer depends on a statute, rule, regulation, or formal legal test. It helps distinguish practical guidance from the legal source of a power or requirement.

Variation
Court Process
A change to an existing court order — adding, removing, or modifying conditions — without cancelling the order entirely. Either party can apply to vary an order if circumstances have changed.
When it applies: This applies when a party is preparing, filing, serving, responding to, or attending a step in family law proceedings. Understanding Variation helps avoid missed deadlines, incomplete material, or confusion about what the court expects next.
Variation Application
Orders
An application to the court seeking to change the terms of an existing order. For parenting orders, the applicant must demonstrate a significant change in circumstances since the original order was made. For financial orders, variation is generally more restricted.
When it applies: This applies when asking the court to make, change, enforce, suspend, or clarify an order. The wording of proposed orders matters because it affects whether obligations are clear and enforceable.

Protection

Court Administration
A party declared by a court to have habitually, persistently, and without reasonable cause instituted vexatious proceedings. A vexatious litigant order restricts the person's ability to file further proceedings without leave of the court.
When it applies: This applies when dealing with the registry, court records, filing systems, listings, sealed documents, or practical case management. It is usually procedural, but mistakes can still delay a matter.
Vexatious Proceedings
Court Process
Court proceedings that are repetitive, baseless or brought for an improper purpose — primarily to harass or exhaust the other party rather than obtain legitimate relief.

Weight of Evidence
Evidence
The persuasive force the court assigns to a piece of evidence when assessing whether a fact has been established. Weight is distinct from admissibility — evidence may be admitted but given little weight. Factors affecting weight include the reliability of the source, corroboration, and the credibility of the witness.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.
Welfare Report
Evidence
A comprehensive report commissioned by the court from a specialist that evaluates the family's circumstances, the needs of the children, the parenting capacity of each parent, and the risks and benefits of proposed arrangements. It includes recommendations for the court.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.
Withholding Allegation
High Conflict
A claim that a parent refused or failed to make a child available for scheduled time with the other parent in breach of a parenting order.
When it applies: This applies where conflict is persistent, communication is unsafe or unproductive, or one party's behaviour affects compliance, parenting, or settlement. Courts look for practical arrangements that reduce risk and protect children from adult conflict.
Without Notice (Ex Parte)
Orders
An application made to the court by one party in the absence of and without prior notification to the other party. Any orders made without notice are temporary, and the absent party must be given an opportunity to be heard and to challenge the orders at a return date.
When it applies: This applies when asking the court to make, change, enforce, suspend, or clarify an order. The wording of proposed orders matters because it affects whether obligations are clear and enforceable.
Without Prejudice
Dispute Resolution
A legal designation applied to communications made in the course of genuine settlement negotiations, protecting them from being tendered as evidence in court proceedings if the negotiations fail. The protection encourages open and frank discussion between parties.
When it applies: This applies when parties are trying to resolve issues by agreement or narrow the dispute before a hearing. It is often cheaper, faster, and less stressful than litigating every issue.
Witness
Evidence
A person who provides evidence in court proceedings, either by way of sworn affidavit filed before the hearing or by giving oral testimony at the hearing. Witnesses may be called by either party and are subject to cross-examination by the opposing party.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.
Witness Statement
Evidence
A written account of facts provided by a witness in support of a party's case, setting out what the witness personally observed or experienced. In family law proceedings, witness statements are typically prepared as affidavits and filed with the court.
When it applies: This applies when a party needs to prove, challenge, organise, or explain facts. Good evidence is specific, relevant, dated where possible, and connected to the orders being sought.
